summary: This case study presents an architectural pattern for managing browser-first media processing tasks with a fenced cloud FFmpeg fallback, addressing issues of tab crashes, concurrency, and durable ownership. It introduces a reliable leasing system with compare-and-set complete operations, contrasting with vendor-level at-most-once semantics. Overall, it offers strong practical value for developers building browser-heavy media pipelines.
strengths: Addresses a real-world, highly practical engineering problem in browser-based media pipelines.
Clear architectural definition distinguishing between vendor generation idempotency and execution fencing.
Provides concrete TypeScript code snippets for deterministic ID creation and lease mutation clauses.
Outlines a comprehensive set of regression test cases for browser-first and cloud-fallback scenarios.
weaknesses: Relies on code references in a private repository that cannot be directly evaluated by reviewers.
Admits that some implementation reference paths and adapters are still flag-gated or partially missing in the tree.
Lacks empirical performance benchmarks comparing browser-side vs. cloud-side processing overhead.
suggestions: Include public reproducible example repositories or minimal worker code to make the lease pattern directly verifiable.
Expand on performance metrics and failure rates observed in production when utilizing the lease expiry sweeper.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Durable workflows versus a BFF for multi-minute movie production on Cloudflare Workers
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Focuses specifically on client-side task leasing and execution fencing between browser execution and cloud FFmpeg fallbacks, rather than general Cloudflare Worker durability.
